newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea bankers grilled in Hanbo Loan scandal.
newsitem.headline: South Korea bankers grilled in Hanbo Loan scandal.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors interrogated the heads of two leading local banks and a former president of a state bank on Tuesday over a loan scandal surrounding insolvent Hanbo Steel Co
With the probe into the scandal widening 10 months before presidential elections, opposition leader Kim Dae-jung urged President Kim Young-sam to quit party politics and concentrate on state affairs.

Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said Sheen Kwang-shik of Korea First Bank, Woo Chan-mok of Cho Hung Bank and Lee Hyung-koo, former chief of the state-run Korea Development Bank, were summoned to his Central Investigation Department.
"Prosecutors are trying to shed light on all suspicions about the loans," Choi said.
Asked by reporters if arrest warrants would be sought for the bankers, Choi said: "That will depend on the outcome of the investigation."
Prosecution officials said the bankers were questioned on whether they received commissions in return for offering huge loans to Hanbo Steel, the country's second largest steelmaker.
The bankers would also be probed if they had faced pressure from politicians or government officials over the loans.

Hanbo Steel, flagship of the Hanbo Group, which is the 14th largest conglomerate in South Korea, piled up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions before it was declared insolvent on January 23.
Finance Ministry officials said Korea First, Cho Hung and Korea Development were Hanbo Steel's three main creditor banks, with combined outstanding loans of 2.4 trillion won.

Choi said that apart from the three being questioned, prosecutors also probed Rhee Chul-soo, a former Korea First Bank president, over the scandal. Rhee was sentenced last August to three years in jail for accepting bribes in return for providing bank loans to other local companies.
President Kim, who ordered a thorough probe into the loans last week, has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.
Prosecutors arrested Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo last Friday on charges of fraud and violating laws on cheques and trust and savings companies.
Kim Dae-jung, seizing on the Hanbo scandal, urged the president to quit his ruling New Korea Party to focus on economic woes and diplomatic affairs.
"The fundamental responsiblity of these loans lie on the (presidential) Blue House," Kim Dae-jung told a news conference.
"If the Blue House did not know about five trillion won of loans, it demonstrates the lack of ability to rule the country. If it knew, then it should be responsible," he said.
The opposition leader accused the government of maintaining a close alliance between politics and business which it condemned as a legacy of the military-backed rule of the past.
Ruling party spokesman Kim Chul said the opposition was trying to capitalise on the crisis to further its politicial ambitions.

Prosecutor Choi said his investigation team was looking into a lobbying fund kept by Chung and possible involvement of politicians in the scandal. Choi's aide said more than 40 bank accounts were traced to find out the size of the fund.
At a weekend meeting with top aides at the Blue House, President Kim expressed frustration over an anti-graft campaign he has been waging since he took office in 1993.
Kim's popularity, which topped 90 percent when he kicked off the anti-corruption drive, has plunged and is now near single digits according to some recent surveys.
In the past year, a defence minister and several of his top officials were arrested for bribery. ($1 = 868 won)
